extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, and judges (readers of patent law doctrine)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and doctrinal tests for what kinds of discoveries, principles, methods, applications, and improvements qualify as patentable subject-matter and how to assess scope and infringement. Focuses on whether a purported invention is an abstract principle, an applied principle, a new use, or merely a double use.

rubrics_metrics.name: No patent for a mere elementary principle or intellectual discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent cannot be for a mere elementary principle, or an intellectual discovery, or a science; principles are elements of science and are not themselves grounds for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principle must be put into practice and applied to some art; the bare discovery of a property of matter or law of physics, without a special and positive application to specific fabrications, is not patentable. (Cited authorities: Boulton v. Bull; Whittemore v. Cutter; Earl v. Sawyer.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent must be for the mode/means of producing an effect, not for the effect alone
rubrics_metrics.description: There cannot be a patent for an effect; the patent must be for the mode or means by which the effect is produced (the practical mode of operating using certain agencies, properties of matter, or laws of physics to produce a given effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims attempting to monopolize an effect rather than a concrete mode or apparatus are invalid. The invention must disclose the means of producing the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle embodied and made active may be patentable as an application
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a principle has been embodied so as to be capable of being made active and to produce an effect, that embodiment (the mode of carrying the principle into effect) may be the subject-matter of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent in such cases is taken for the mode of carrying the principle into effect. If another puts the principle to use in a substantially identical adaptation aimed at the same end, that may be infringement (jury question). (See discussion of embodiment and §78.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot claim an abstract art or principle in the large — claims must be confined
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that purports to cover an art or principle in the abstract (for example, claiming the art of cutting ice by any non-human power) is unmaintainable; claims must be confined to particular methods, machinery, or modes disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A too-broad functional/omnibus claim (covering all means to an end) is invalid; a timely disclaimer may sometimes salvage narrower aspects. Example: Wyeth v. Stone (cutting ice claim invalid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents may protect against colorable variations if they implement the same principle to the same end
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee has invented some mode of carrying a principle into effect, he is entitled to protection against other modes that are merely colorable variations of that mode and which apply the same principle to achieve the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In infringement, the question is whether the defendant has undertaken to carry the same principle into effect in the same mode in substance, notwithstanding differences of form or appliances (jury issue). (Cited: Jupe v. Pratt; Neilson v. Harford; Gray v. James.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Two broad classes of patentable cases: new application of known agents vs discovery/application of new agents
rubrics_metrics.description: One class covers new applications of known agents/things that change the series of processes or produce a new result; the other covers discovery and application of new agents or things that produce a new effect or result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification when analyzing whether a claimed subject-matter is patentable; examples include use of electricity for telegraphy or application of light for photography (may fall in either class depending on facts). (§82)

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapting a known substance or agent to a particular purpose can be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The adaptation and application of a natural or known agent, substance, or thing to produce a given effect may be the subject-matter of a patent (e.g., immersing manufactured cloth in hot water; preparing paper surface with white lead and size).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the agent is known, a new preparation, omission of an ingredient, or new ordering of process steps producing a useful and vendible result can constitute a new manufacture. Examples: Daniell, Fusell, Christ's copperplate printing, water-proofing fabrics by new sequences. (§81, §82)

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement in the mode of producing a known effect may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements or inventions in the mode of producing a particular known effect can be patentable subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hartley's plates to protect buildings from fire; Forsyth's application of detonating powder as priming. The improvement must itself be new and not merely trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical test for application-of-principle cases: agents, method, and result
rubrics_metrics.description: When a principle's application is asserted, analyze (1) whether the agents employed are newly discovered or well known, (2) whether they are applied in a new method, and (3) whether they produce, as applied, a new or an old result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these three inquiries to determine the patentable character of the invention or discovery. The distinction between a principle and its practice is central. (§84)

rubrics_metrics.name: Double use doctrine — mere new occasion analogous to old use is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: If a principle is well known and the new application is merely a 'double use' (a new occasion analogous to previously known uses), that new application is not patentable; it is only a double use of a known thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations include known medicines used for another disease (mere new occasion), use of an old process on a new but analogous object (palm leaf vs hair), or applying known wheels to railways where analogy is close. The new use must not be merely analogous to escape the double-use bar. (§85–87)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between applying a new contrivance to an old object and an old contrivance to a new object
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a new contrivance to an old object may be patentable, but applying an old contrivance to a new object (when the new object is merely analogous to previous objects) is generally not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court examples and jury instructions illustrate this nuance (Losh v. Hague; Lord Abinger's reasoning). The novelty must reside in more than mere change of context if the contrivance is old.

rubrics_metrics.name: New effect vs new occasion: only new effect supports patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: When a known thing is used, determine whether the effect produced is itself entirely new, or whether only the occasion/use is new; only a genuinely new effect (not merely a new occasion) supports patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only the occasion is new and the effect is analogous to prior uses, the claim is likely a double use and invalid; if the effect is novel (no known analogous uses), it may be patentable. (§88)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be tied to described machinery/mode; overbroad functional claiming is invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification that describes a particular machine or mode supports a patent for that specific structure or mode; claiming a mere function detached from machinery or claiming all possible modes to achieve a function is insufficient and may render the claim void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Blanchard v. Sprague and Story's analysis — patent claims should identify the particular machine or mode; claiming only a function in the abstract is inadequate. A patentee should describe how the invention is to be constructed and operated to define scope. (§85 note)
